item.title: Trusted AI by design, not by default
item.description:
As AI adoption accelerates, mounting concerns over rogue AI agents, potential data and privacy breaches, and other security risks have companies doubling down on safeguards and governance strategies intended to build trust in enterprise AI.

The Hugging Face incident, where OpenAI agents escaped their testing sandbox, and other well-publicized breaches have sharpened attention to the importance of guardrails to rein in agentic AI. More specifically, these episodes highlight the need for governance and security checkpoints to be built directly into enterprise AI workflows as part of strategic design—not bolted on post-deployment.

“The recent AI hacking incidents show that AI can infiltrate any part of the software supply chain and data to exploit your weakness,” notes Ali Khorso, a partner solutions engineer at Snowflake. “There must be more emphasis on AI security, not just on LLMs, but on the whole supply chain.”

A partnership grounded in trust

Snowflake and Google Cloud have made trusted AI a cornerstone of their long-standing partnership. Security and governance are deeply rooted in the Snowflake DNA, with the AI Data Cloud’s built-in governance, security, and cross-cloud sharing capabilities working in tandem to safeguard enterprise AI workloads.

As the “guardian” of enterprise data, Snowflake’s first principle is to bring services directly to where enterprise data lives, enforced through its zero-copy technology, which doesn’t move or duplicate anything. Native integration of Google Cloud’s Gemini models directly within the Snowflake Cortex AI framework leverages this approach to allow customers to build, run, and scale AI workflows with established governance and security policies without an additional data management burden.

Snowflake and Google Cloud support secure and trusted AI in a variety of other ways, including:

Robust, built-in security

Google Cloud is known for its robust and secure ecosystem and networks, and the partners employ security-by-design safeguards on top of that rich foundation. Snowflake Horizon, a catalog and built-in suite of data governance, security, and compliance tools, uses a Role-Based Access Control (RBAC) framework to grant permissions by role, in addition to data lineage functionality for tracking data throughout its lifecycle and masking capabilities to ensure users don’t see any data they are not supposed to.

Governance and enterprise context

Snowflake’s Cortex AI Gateway is a centralized MCP gateway that enforces identity, policy, and access at the tool-call level. The platform serves as an interoperability layer that helps govern how AI agents access and use LLMs, leveraging the full context of the enterprise and in support of a distributed intelligence model.

There is also secure, bi-directional integration with Google Cloud and AI services through an open lakehouse architecture, which ensures universal governance and security policies persist across platforms.

Resiliency and continuity

Given the growing number of security exploits, business continuity remains a pressing issue in the agentic era. Snowflake and Google Cloud’s cross-cloud support ensures robust failover and recovery services. Organizations simply establish backup zones and clouds, and workloads are automatically redirected in the event of an issue.

As hackers embrace AI to uplevel their own exploits, security and trust loom large. Snowflake and Google Cloud’s commitment to a secure-by-design approach empowers enterprises to move confidently forward and reap the rewards of AI success.

item.title: Keep skyrocketing AI costs in check
item.description:
The rapid rise of AI has introduced another challenge for IT leaders: How to effectively manage surging compute and infrastructure costs with an eye towards optimizing spend and achieving demonstrable ROI.

Expensive AI infrastructure, rising development costs, and token-based pricing models are helping to drive up the AI price tag, often to levels that are higher than expected. Agentic AI takes a greater toll on costs as models use between 5 and 30 times more tokens per task than standard chatbots.

By 2028, Gartner predicts AI coding costs will overtake the average developer’s salary due to surging LLM token consumption and the shift to consumption-based licensing models. A FinOps Foundation survey identified managing the cost and use of tokens in SaaS-model AI as the top challenge facing practitioners today.

“Agents have blown out the cost of everything,” says Rachel Roundy, principal product marketing manager for AI at Snowflake. “Companies are at a point where they are weighing the pros and cons of how much value they are getting out of the agentic toolset versus how much they are paying for it. They are looking for ways to find cost efficiencies.”

A trifecta for keeping costs in check

Compared to cloud compute workloads, AI tasks stack up costs more quickly depending on the model and prompt iteration cycle, creating budgeting and forecasting challenges. Snowflake, in tandem with partner Google Cloud, delivers capabilities and services to help optimize AI economics and bring predictability to deployments. Among them

Budget and cost controls. Snowflake establishes transparency and trust on the cost front in a variety of ways. Highly granular views of daily AI spend provide visibility into adoption patterns and AI usage across business units so quick adjustments can be made. User quotas and group budgeting capabilities allow organizations to set spending limits for defined groups of users and resources while triggering automated and programmable cost enforcement. “This gives customers the ability to put in guardrails to curtail runaway spending that might accrue,” says Pranav Pokharel, Snowflake’s principal product manager.

Model flexibility. Not every use case calls for the most advanced frontier models—simpler, well-defined tasks can run efficiently on open and smaller models. Snowflake’s AI Data Cloud gives customers the freedom to choose among leading open and proprietary models, including Google Cloud’s full lineup. With dynamic model routing capabilities in Cortex AI Gateway, enterprises can select the right model for a specific job. They simply define approved models and specify trade-offs, and the platform evaluates each task against policies and real-world cost and performance data. This ensures the model is matched to the task with optimized spend.

Harness architecture tuned for optimization. The harness for Snowflake CoCo and Snowflake CoWork agents is essential to lowering the AI bill. The harness loads tools and skills on demand, bundling independent tool calls into a single dispatch, which compacts tool output and ensures fewer model calls. The harness also gives agents the necessary context that would otherwise have to be discovered. This helps reduce context bloat while resulting in fewer turns and tokens.

As enterprises eyeball mounting AI costs, they should approach fiscal governance as an enabler, not a hurdle to AI adoption. “Governing costs doesn’t mean you’re inhibiting innovation in the company,” Pokharel says. “It should make you more confident in how you orchestrate AI rollouts.”

item.title: Rewrite the rules of enterprise recovery
item.description:
For decades, recovery has followed a predictable path rooted in Information Technology Infrastructure Library (ITIL) processes, and although the enterprise stack has grown ever more complex with each passing year, the traditional model has largely served organizations well.

AI is upending that model. On top of handling an already sprawling set of applications and data, organizations must now restore models, training data, agent workflows, and pipelines that span on-premises, cloud, and SaaS environments. These pieces depend heavily on each other, with metadata tying them together. Get one element wrong or restore it without that context, and the result may look complete but fail to produce reliable output.

To illustrate, let’s imagine a company that restores its recommendation model after a ransomware attack. Because the metadata, checkpoint, and preprocessing scripts aren’t from the same point in time, the dashboard shows green while recommendations drift off target, causing revenue to fall. Just as bad, if a hidden threat resides within the recovery point, the restore can bring the attack back with it.

Organizations believe they’re prepared, but the data tells another story. According to SINC research, 94% of organizations believe that their disaster recovery plans cover AI but only one in 10 has tested and documented recovery of an AI system from a verified clean backup. This means that most organizations’ first AI recovery will take place during a real incident.

Build a repeatable recovery process for AI through testing and ownership

Preparation starts with tests under real-world pressure. Tests should verify that the recovery point is clean and confirm that supporting systems such as vector databases and registries work, and they should include a scenario where AI data has been tampered with.

Ownership also matters. With business units building agents, IT running infrastructure, and Security monitoring threats, responsibility for recoverability often falls to no one. One accountable executive, often the CISO with support from the CIO, should own the program. Additionally, each critical AI service needs a named business owner who defines how much disruption the business can tolerate.

Use AI to automate and validate AI recovery

AI is far too complex for manual recovery, so the recovery process itself needs AI to ensure that it is continuous, complete, clean, and confirmed. In AI-assisted recovery, AI handles the discovery, tagging, and policy enforcement that keep protection current. When new agents or data sources appear, AI finds them, protects them, and schedules recovery tests. And because completeness depends on restoring the full AI stack as a coherent unit, AI constantly maps dependencies across the stack and orchestrates workflows that bring everything back in the right order.

Clean recovery requires ensuring that no threats lie hidden in backups. AI hunts for threats in backup data and pinpoints the last clean recovery point. If recent backups contain files that have been tampered with, AI can build a composite recovery point from the most recent clean version of each file. Confirmation closes the loop. AI can provision isolated spaces where teams can safely validate a restore before it reaches production.

Commvault AI Recovery brings these capabilities together. Newly released capabilities such as AgentRecover make AI tools, data, and the systems around them more recoverable. AI-enabled Cleanpoint validation, Synthetic Recovery, and Commvault Cleanroom work together to ensure that organizations can both recover at machine speed and trust that the restored AI is clean and complete. With AI assisting in AI recovery, organizations can overcome the challenges this new technology presents to disaster recovery professionals, ensuring that the business doesn’t suffer lasting damage when a disaster occurs.

item.title: Tether solves the memory challenge for AI builders who don’t want to rely on the cloud
item.description:
Thanks to the rise of a new generation of highly capable small AI models, on-device or local inference has become increasingly viable for a greater range of applications.

However, limited memory capacity often prevents local AI from reaching its full potential. A model that fits comfortably on a laptop or phone can hit a wall the moment it has to hold a long conversation or search a large database.

To advance on-device AI capabilities, Tether’s QVAC SDK tackles the memory challenge from two directions.

By integrating TurboQuant and TurboVec, the software development kit shrinks two of the biggest memory costs in a local AI pipeline: the model’s working memory during inference, and the index it searches when answering questions from your own documents.

Compressing what AI remembers  

Modern language models generate text through a process called self-attention, in which each token (the basic units of text) gets encoded into three vectors: a query, a key, and a value. The query is what the current token is “looking for”; the key is what each earlier token offers up to be matched against that query; and the value is the actual content pulled forward once a match is found.

AI models don’t reprocess the whole conversation for every new word. They keep a running store of key and value projections for every token already seen: the KV cache.

Originally developed by Google researchers, TurboQuant is an open-source compression algorithm for this KV cache that transforms 16- or 32-bit vectors into smaller ones, without losing too much accuracy. The result is up to a five times reduction in the amount of memory used to store context during inference.

Reducing the size of a model’s KV cache enables AI running on consumer hardware to process longer context prompts that would otherwise exceed local memory capacity.

Consider a four billion parameter model like Qwen3.5-4B running at 262,000 tokens of context.

While the model weights alone are small enough to fit on a smartphone’s VRAM, with that context, a standard 16-bit KV cache would balloon to around 8 GB.

Accounting for the model itself and the necessary overhead, that’s more than what the average consumer GPU can handle.

In contrast, by applying TurboQuant to the same model, a 262,000 token KV cache is reduced to a much more manageable 1.6 GB.

This orientation toward everyday hardware is exactly what Tether is targeting with QVAC. For instance, TurboQuant was integrated into QVAC SDK v0.12.0 with Windows and Linux support for machines equipped with NVIDIA, AMD, and Intel GPUs.

Compressing what AI searches  

While applying TurboQuant to a model’s KV cache streamlines AI inference, another tool in the QVAC SDK, TurboVec, applies the same quantization algorithm to a different bottleneck: vector indexing.

To respond to user queries, modern AI tools aren’t limited to knowledge contained within their training data; they can also search for relevant information on the internet or specific databases using a technique known as retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).

To enable this search, the system turns text into vectors, then orders them so vectors with similar meaning sit close together. Each search then compares your question’s vector against the stored ones and returns passages of text with the closest values.

After applying TurboVec, ten million typical embedding vectors shrink from roughly 61GB to about 8GB. In terms of the necessary RAM, that’s the difference between an expensive custom setup and a standard desktop computer.

In its original form, TurboVec was an open-source Rust project developed by Ryan Codrai, but QVAC doesn’t depend on that Rust code. Instead, the Tether team implemented the same quantizer natively in their own stack, equipping SDK users with another powerful compression tool to boost speed and reduce memory requirements.

One algorithm, two efficiency boosts  

For QVAC, TurboQuant and TurboVec apply the same compression math to different ends of the AI pipeline. One shrinks the memory a model uses while it thinks. The other shrinks the memory it searches to find what to think about. For anyone trying to run AI on a desktop or smartphone, the respective VRAM and RAM savings mean greater capabilities for memory-constrained devices.

By bringing RAG on to everyday edge devices, apps can plug into sensitive databases without users having to worry about potential leaks. AI can recall its own usage data and agent memory, or private documents such as legal or medical records without uploading anything to the cloud.

Reducing cloud dependency can also save money. When every gigabyte TurboQuant and TurboVec claw back is a gigabyte that doesn’t have to be rented from a cloud provider, the long-term cost savings are significant.

Now & Next brings that ecosystem into one conversation.

Healthcare leaders must protect sensitive data without interrupting care. Financial institutions face rigorous governance and audits. Public-sector organizations confront sophisticated threats. Manufacturers must secure access without slowing production.

Operational technology brings a different set of priorities to endpoint strategy. On the plant floor, in control rooms, and across critical infrastructure, uptime, resilience, and secure access matter differently because disruption can stop operations.

As IT and OT converge, the OT track at Now & Next will explore how organizations can strengthen endpoint trust, governance, segmentation, and operational resilience without adding unnecessary complexity.

item.title: Why CIOs must make zero trust an AI-era priority in 2027
item.description:
AI is moving from generating information to taking action. AI agents can access data, invoke applications and APIs, and interact with business systems on behalf of users. For CIOs, that changes the security question. Verifying an identity is only the beginning. Organizations also need to govern what an agent is authorized to do once access has been granted, and what happens if it attempts an action outside those boundaries.

In its analysis of the 2026 Cost of a Data Breach report, IBM found that 21% of organizations studied reported a security incident involving an AI model or application. Among those organizations, 92% lacked proper AI access controls.

Zero trust offers a way to tackle these risks by always checking who’s involved, what device they’re using, where they’re working from, and what they’re trying to do. With this approach, organizations can let people and AI use the tools they need while continuously verifying access and enforcing policy as conditions change.

Access decisions need context

Putting that principle into practice involves more than verifying identity. A developer may be authorized to access source code, but not to copy it into an unapproved AI service. An autonomous agent may be allowed to analyze customer records, but not to export them, change permissions, or initiate transactions.

These decisions depend on context, including device condition, application sensitivity, session risk, the tools being invoked, and the potential impact of the requested action.

AI innovation and AI security cannot be an either/or decision. Organizations need guardrails that allow autonomy to expand as their ability to govern it improves. That means establishing the trust, policy, and runtime controls needed to keep agents operating within defined authority, while allowing legitimate work to continue.

A trusted endpoint is essential to zero trust

Identity and network controls can verify connections and manage access, but they may not fully address endpoint configuration, local data protection, or workload control. Writable systems, stored credentials, and broad application footprints can increase exposure to persistent threats, credential theft, and unauthorized code, even when other controls are working as intended.

CIOs should consider whether their organizations can maintain a trusted endpoint state, limit local data, govern workloads, and adapt the workspace as risk changes. Endpoints are more than a place to launch applications. They are an important link between identity, workspace, applications, and data.

Protect the complete access path

The browser is increasingly the front door to SaaS applications, cloud consoles, virtual desktops, AI copilots, and agents. This is blurring the boundaries between endpoint, browser, identity, network, application, and data security.

Each layer can work well on its own and still leave gaps between controls. An identity platform may verify a user’s identity even if their device has been compromised. A secure access service may protect the connection, yet sensitive information can still be copied into an unapproved application.

A mature zero trust architecture can help coordinate these controls. If a device falls out of compliance, the organization may need to restrict the session. If an AI agent invokes an unauthorized tool, the organization should be able to stop that action without disrupting legitimate workflows.

For CIOs, the priority is making these controls work as a coordinated architecture. Identity establishes who or what is requesting access. Device and application context inform what should be permitted. Policy enforcement must then happen at the appropriate point, whether that’s the endpoint, network, browser, or application. These controls need to work together as conditions change.

Resilience belongs in zero trust

A trusted endpoint can strengthen a zero trust strategy. IGEL OS™ uses an immutable, read-only architecture designed to help reduce attack surface and unauthorized changes. At the same time, IGEL Adaptive Secure Desktop™ provides a governed workspace experience aligned with user needs and enterprise policy.

When ransomware, a failed Windows update, or another disruption affects endpoint access, IGEL Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery™ can provide an alternate, controlled path to approved applications and workspaces. On supported, preconfigured endpoints, IGEL Dual Boot™ and IGEL Emergency Mode™ enable administrators to transition users into IGEL OS™ while the Windows partition remains isolated and preserved for investigation and remediation by IT and security teams.

Prioritize zero trust controls and endpoint resilience in 2027

For CIOs, the 2027 priority is to invest in the controls that allow AI adoption to advance safely. As agents gain the ability to act across enterprise systems, organizations need clear limits on their authority, trusted execution environments, and the ability to monitor, restrict, or interrupt unauthorized actions. Greater autonomy should follow the organization’s ability to govern it.

This requires coordinated identity controls, ongoing verification, secure application delivery, and an endpoint foundation that limits persistence and local data exposure while adapting to each session. It also requires a safe, controlled way for employees to access critical applications during ransomware attacks, failed updates, or operating system outages.

In the age of AI, zero trust needs to reach the endpoint, too. The IGEL Adaptive Secure Endpoint Platform™ provides an immutable, centrally governed endpoint foundation with limited local data exposure. It works alongside existing identity, network, browser, and application investments, supporting policy-aligned access and helping restore secure access when Windows endpoints are disrupted.

item.title: Beyond RTO: Why CIOs should measure time to restored user access
item.description:
Meeting an RTO does not necessarily mean the business has recovered. CIOs should also measure how long it takes authorized users to resume critical workflows through approved access paths.

A system can be back online while the business remains offline.

An electronic health record might be available, but clinicians still might not be able to access it. A transaction platform could be running, but service teams may have trouble using it. A manufacturing application could be working, but plant operators might not be able to connect while devices are being checked or replaced.

Recovery Time Objective, or RTO, tells us how long it should take to restore systems to operation. But CIOs also need to look at what really happens for users: how fast employees can get back to their important tasks.

Address the endpoint access recovery gap

Many organizations spend a lot on backup systems and recovery tools. Still, plans often overlook the actual devices people use to connect to those resources.

If ransomware, a failed update, a Windows outage, or another issue affects endpoints, IT teams often need to check, fix, or swap out devices. Sometimes, new hardware needs to be set up and sent out.

These steps can add a lot of time, sometimes hours or even days, after main services are back up.

This leads to a gap between when a service is back up and when people can actually use it again. The real question isn’t just about meeting the RTO; it’s about when staff can start working as usual.

Measure what users actually experience

One useful way to make this distinction visible is to measure Recovery Time Actual, or RTA, alongside RTO.

RTO asks: How quickly should a service be restored?

RTA asks: How long did it actually take employees to regain trusted access and get back to work?

RTA is a practical operational measure: the time it actually takes for someone to get back to work after an incident. It doesn’t replace RTO or act as a one-size-fits-all industry metric. Instead, it shows the difference between the goal and what really happens.

That measurement might include declaring an incident, starting recovery, ensuring devices are ready, checking the network, logging in, opening the needed apps, and verifying that people can do their work.

Looking at the bigger picture can show problems that usual recovery reports miss. Sometimes, an application is up, but identity services aren’t. A user might log in but can’t use a needed device. What works on one computer might not work everywhere, especially when lots of different devices are involved.

CIOs should therefore consider measuring actual user-access recovery by persona, workflow, site, and scale.

Decouple workforce recovery from Windows remediation

For CIOs, the objective is not necessarily to accelerate every step of endpoint remediation. It is to establish a prepared path back to critical services while security and IT teams address the affected Windows environment.

A compromised Windows device may need to remain untouched for forensic investigation. That shouldn’t mean the employee has to remain unable to work.

An endpoint-access continuity model can help separate those timelines. IGEL Business Continuity & Disaster Recovery™ (IGEL BC&DR™) supports this approach by providing an alternative, policy-controlled path via IGEL OS™ for authorized users to access approved, available services. Depending on the organization’s preparation and requirements, IGEL Dual Boot™, together with IGEL Emergency Mode™, can enable authorized administrators to centrally direct selected, supported IGEL Dual Boot™-enabled devices into IGEL OS™. IGEL USB Boot™ provides a separately prepared, externally booted option for supported devices.

This approach does not recover applications, data, networks, identity systems, or the Windows environment. It complements those recovery efforts by addressing the endpoint-access layer between available services and the people who need to reach them.

CIOs should focus on being prepared. Recovery plans need to be developed, tested, and validated for different users, tasks, locations, and devices. The actual time it takes to recover will depend on factors such as the hardware used, whether the right settings are in place, available licenses, network and identity access, and how everything is set up.

Connect RTA to critical workflows

Actual user-access recovery becomes meaningful when tied to a defined operational outcome.

In healthcare, for example, the measure may be the time required for an authorized clinician to access an approved patient-care workflow, including available electronic health records, communications, imaging services, authentication systems, and supported peripherals.

In financial services, it can reflect authorized access to systems supporting branch operations, customer service, transaction processing, trading, ERP, or communications.

In manufacturing, RTA may be defined around supported workflows involving plant-floor workstations, logistics systems, engineering applications, control-room access, and operator communications. Planning may also need to account for rugged hardware, limited-bandwidth sites, specialized peripherals, local applications, and operational technology dependencies.

Government agencies and critical-industry organizations can define RTA by mission and role, such as access to approved applications supporting public services, emergency communications, or critical operations.

Make RTA an executive measure

For CIOs, the question isn’t simply whether recovery met its target. It’s whether employees could actually resume critical work. CIOs should incorporate user-access recovery into business impact analysis and define a minimum viable recovery workspace for each priority role.

Testing should measure the complete journey back to an approved, operationally meaningful workflow, rather than stopping when a device starts or an application becomes available. It should also examine recovery across a distributed workforce, recognizing that initiating recovery centrally does not mean every user can resume work at the same time.

Reporting average and slowest user-access recovery times alongside RTO helps leaders identify which roles, locations, or workflows still face recovery gaps.

Shift from technical recovery to operational continuity

RTO remains essential, but it is not the whole measure of continuity.

Just because an app is running again doesn’t mean patient care, customer service, or production is back to normal. People need a simple, reliable way to reach the systems they use every day.

By measuring and rehearsing actual user-access recovery alongside RTO, CIOs can identify the endpoint, identity, network, application, and operational dependencies that determine when the organization has truly recovered.

item.title: Adaptability in action: How CIOs can modernize work without sacrificing resilience
item.description:
IT modernization rarely follows a straight path. New SaaS and cloud-delivered services often work alongside virtual desktops, specialized applications, and critical Windows workloads. Meanwhile, employees need secure, reliable access wherever they work.

For CIOs, this creates a strategic challenge: How can the organization modernize at different speeds without creating a separate endpoint strategy for every workload?

That question will be a key topic of discussion at IGEL Now & Next 2027, taking place Feb. 16 through 18 in Fort Lauderdale, Florida. The event will bring together IT and security leaders, architects, practitioners, and technology partners to explore more adaptable approaches to secure digital work.

Turn adaptability into an operational capability

Addressing this challenge begins by turning adaptability from a strategic ambition into an operational capability. Adaptability is easy to endorse but harder to put into practice. It requires an architecture that supports multiple application-delivery models without forcing IT to rebuild the endpoint environment whenever business requirements change.

A SaaS service can run in a browser. Graphics-heavy workloads may be better suited to VDI or DaaS, while production environments often use native or containerized applications. Some critical Windows applications may still need a managed Windows environment.

Supporting this variety is only part of the equation. IT must also maintain a coherent user experience and consistent governance across those delivery models.

Few enterprises can modernize every application at once. CIOs require an endpoint strategy that meets current end-user needs while allowing for future evolution. Adaptability is not about adding more tools; it is about enabling changes to how work is performed without redesigning the underlying environment.

Build a stable endpoint foundation for changing environments

That ability to accommodate change depends on identifying which parts of the environment should remain stable. Not every part of the technology environment should remain in motion. A stable endpoint foundation allows IT teams to evolve applications, delivery models, and workspace experiences without repeatedly rebuilding the underlying environment.

An immutable, centrally governed approach can help limit configuration drift and local data exposure while supporting secure access across a changing application portfolio. IGEL applies these principles to help organizations build an endpoint foundation that works with existing identity, management, and security investments.

Support multiple paths to productivity across delivery models

With that foundation in place, IT can support multiple paths to productivity without allowing any one delivery model to determine the entire endpoint strategy.

CIOs should avoid allowing a single application-delivery model to dictate their endpoint strategy. A flexible architecture can support SaaS, browsers, VDI and DaaS, native applications, and essential Windows workloads while delivering a consistent, well-governed user experience.

The goal is not to preserve every delivery model. It is to give IT the flexibility to modernize each workload at the right pace without repeatedly redesigning the endpoint environment.

Design continuity around workforce access

The value of this flexibility becomes especially clear when normal operations are disrupted. Disruption reveals whether adaptability is truly built into the operating model. For CIOs, the critical question is not only how quickly systems can be recovered, but how quickly employees can safely resume essential work.

That requires separating workforce access from infrastructure recovery. By establishing a governed, alternative path to critical applications before an incident, organizations can maintain productivity while remediation proceeds independently.

Viewed this way, continuity becomes an extension of the endpoint and application-access strategy. It becomes an architectural capability rather than a response improvised during a crisis.

Build an operating model for continuous change

Building these capabilities requires more than the right architecture. It also requires organizational alignment. Technology alone does not create adaptability. CIOs must align security, application, infrastructure, and business-continuity leaders around four strategic questions:

  • Which delivery model best fits each workload?
  • Which applications are priorities for modernization?
  • Which services must remain accessible during disruption?
  • How can users receive a consistent experience as conditions change?

Answering these questions turns individual technology choices into a coordinated road map for adaptability.

Join a community built around what comes next

The future of secure digital work spans disciplines, technologies, and organizations. No single product or provider can address every challenge. Meaningful progress requires leaders, practitioners, and technology partners to work across traditional boundaries.

IGEL Now & Next 2027 brings that community together to share practical lessons, evaluate emerging approaches, and build digital work environments that can evolve with changing applications and business needs.

item.title: OX Security Launches OX Radar and Response Center to Show Companies Which Cyber Threats Actually Affect Them
item.description:
New technology monitors critical vulnerabilities and supply chain threats, automatically assessing customer exposure and guiding remediation

OX Security, a leader in AI-native application protection, today announced the launch of OX Radar and Response Center, giving security teams one place to track high-priority cyber threats, determine whether their organizations are affected, and manage remediation.

OX Radar continuously monitors emerging vulnerabilities, compromised software dependencies, and actively exploited threats. Integrated with OX Security’s application security platform, the Response Center automatically checks supported threats against customer environments, identifying affected assets and providing the context and guidance needed to respond. Separately, a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed provides broader security research and findings across the software and AI supply chain.

When a major vulnerability or supply chain attack emerges, security teams often spend hours searching advisories, checking inventories, and correlating findings across tools to answer the question that matters most: Are we affected? As new software and AI components proliferate, investigating every potential threat manually is becoming increasingly impractical.

“The question isn’t just whether a new threat is dangerous. It’s whether it’s dangerous to you,” said Neatsun Ziv, CEO and co-founder of OX Security. “AI is accelerating software development, expanding the supply chain, and generating more security alerts than teams can realistically investigate. Security teams need to know immediately which threats affect their organization, which don’t, and what action is required.”

From Breaking Threats to Customer Action

To help security teams stay ahead of threats requiring urgent attention, OX Radar scans CVE databases, known-exploited vulnerability catalogs, security advisories, and vendor research approximately every 10 minutes. The customer-facing capabilities focus on high-priority threats, including compromised or malicious dependencies, exploited vulnerabilities, and critical-severity CVEs.

The Response Center connects supported OX Radar threats to each customer’s environment, checking whether vulnerable components are present and assessing their exploitability. It combines intelligence from the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) and the European Union Agency for Cybersecurity (ENISA) Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalogs, EPSS exploit predictions, and VEX exploitability status with OX Security’s AI-generated exploit checks and runtime visibility to determine whether vulnerable libraries are affected.

Through the Response Center, security teams can:

  • Track threats: Follow high-priority incidents as new intelligence and findings emerge.
  • Assess exposure: Identify affected assets and examine supporting evidence.
  • Prioritize risk: Evaluate severity, exploitation, code usage, and reachability.
  • Manage remediation: Access safe versions and guidance, and create or track tickets and fix pull requests.
  • Document response: Maintain records of findings and remediation activity.

For each supported incident, the Response Center indicates whether a vulnerability has been detected in the customer’s environment, provides evidence of its potential exploitability, and incorporates available VEX information to help teams determine whether action is required. Teams can also initiate investigations using a CVE identifier, GitHub Security Advisory identifier, or advisory URL.

Expanding Threat Visibility Through Public Research

Alongside the customer-facing capabilities, OX Security is introducing a publicly accessible OX Radar threat feed with a broader catalog of security findings. Powered by OX Security’s independent research and scanning, the feed analyzes newly published npm and PyPI packages, AI skills, and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers.

OX Security will continue expanding the range of threats assessed against customer environments, bringing more findings from its public research into the Response Center over time.

Availability

OX Radar and Response Center are available to OX Security customers as part of OX Security’s AI-Native Application Protection Platform (AINAPP). The broader OX Radar research feed is publicly accessible through the OX Security website.

About OX Security

OX Security is the first AI-Native Application Protection Platform built to secure software from prompt to production runtime. Its platform includes VibeSec, OX Code, OX Cloud, and OX Agentic Pentester, giving security teams a unified system for securing AI-driven development, applications, and cloud environments.

item.title: What is a semantic knowledge graph, and does your AI need one?
item.description:
A traditional database organizes information into tables. One column is the name, another is the company they work for. A graph database stores the same information not in tables but in nodes and edges. A person could be one node, the company they work for is another, and the edge is the connection between the two.

Any node can be connected to any other one, making graph databases much more flexible. And finding related entities is as simple as following the edges from one node to another. They’re useful for navigating supply chain dependencies, detecting fraud, or mapping user preferences to make better recommendations.

All of that is already potentially useful to AI agents, but that’s not all. A knowledge graph sits on top of the graph database and is a map of the relationships. The node with the person’s name, for example, could be connected to the node with the company information because the person is an employee of that company. The knowledge graph helps explain what the data is.

A semantic graph, or a semantic knowledge graph, takes this one step further and adds a deeper level of meaning. For example, the list of companies could actually be a list of clients or potential clients. The list of people could also be potential contacts for sales calls, and their job titles could indicate their relative importance.

The semantic layer is all about what the data means for the enterprise and how the data is actually used in practice. When AI agents are assigned actual work tasks, they need to have this information.

“Agentic AI is AI that can do things, not just tell you things,” says Rafael Domene, global CIO at manufacturing company Cosentino. “But you have to provide what AI needs to do the job in the right way. Not just data, but information. It’s about business knowledge and understanding what’s going on.”

Cosentino had already invested a lot of money into a massive data lake and data lakehouse, as well as ERP and CRM systems. “You can collect all the data, but that’s not enough to explain what’s going on,” he says. “If a KPI goes red, you need to dive deep into the organization to understand what happened.” Traditionally, that means human experts with a deep understanding of how the company works. So how can this process be automated with AI? The semantic layer gives AI the business context behind the data.

Justified layering

Historically, building this semantic layer has been a tough job. It requires subject matter experts, and it’s not a one-and-done project since the way a company does things changes constantly. It usually wasn’t worth the effort, especially if the analysts looking at the data already had the context to understand what it meant due to their knowledge of the company. They didn’t need a semantic layer because they had their own human understanding.

AI agents, however? Not so much. Not only do they have a bad understanding of how companies work in general, but they also don’t know much about how any one company works in particular.

Cosentino began building its semantic layer three years ago and aims to be finished by the end of the year. “The main processes and flows are already there, and the remaining work is mostly on the financial side of the business, including logistics, manufacturing, operations, customer service and sales, procurement, and HR.

The effort is already showing results, he says. Take for example a delayed order. “Service levels for our customers are really important,” says Domene. “But there are 15 departments involved in the process and all of them had their own dashboards. We were having a lot of issues finding out last minute that a specific order wasn’t going to be served.”

Now an AI agent can look at any order, for any customer, and predict whether it’ll arrive on time or be delayed. And if there is a delay, where the holdup is.

“If the raw materials don’t arrive on time, or the factory has an issue, the process isn’t going to reach the customer on time,” he says. But if the salesperson knows about the problem as soon as it happens, they can go back to the customer, explain what happened, and offer potential solutions.

“It’s not just about providing information,” says Domene. “Without context, I can’t link things. What happens with this process, why is this order different from the previous one, why is this happening, what can I do, and what’s the best course of action so we can make the right decision for this customer or product?”

Or, say a customer exceeded a credit limit and an order was blocked. In the past, that would result in an average delay of 22 days. Today, the maximum length of delay is one day.

“This is a service and performance improvement,” he says. “There was a team of people in the finance department doing those things. And now they’re free from it all, doing things that are more vital for our customers.”

According to Domene, the company saw up to $10 million in savings in the first year of the project. “The return was really fast,” he says, “and the benefits are way beyond more savings. It also impacts our revenues.”

By the end of the year, he says, the company expects to get to $100 million in savings. And there are other benefits. For example, sales employees used to spend more than a third of their time on administrative work, and they’ll soon have AI agents assisting them in those tasks. Cosentino began building those agents last year, testing them this year, and expects to have them fully operational soon.

“Not all of that saved time is going to be turned into revenue,” Domene says. “We’ll see how much we get out of that, but we see massive potential.”

When the knowledge graph and semantic layer process began, it was largely a manual process, managed by the company’s own expert employees, and combined with a group of engineers from the vendor the company chose for the project, process mining company Celonis.

“Systems like SAP have fixed flows and context so it was relatively easy,” Domene says. “But it still required effort by humans.” Then, over time, AI was added to augment the humans.

Still, the process of building the semantic layer isn’t yet ready to be fully automated.

“Humans don’t always create documents in ways the AI can understand semantic relationships,” says David Hoelzer, a fellow at the SANS Institute, and chief of operations at Enclave Forensics.

AI can help accelerate the process of building the knowledge graph, he says, and it can help keep it up to date. But it’d be a mistake to let the AI try to build completely on its own. “It may end up with relationships that don’t make sense,” he says. “You still need people and they need a very particular set of skills.”

Knowledge graphs versus vector databases

About a year ago, the standard way to feed new information into an LLM was via RAG in combination with vector databases. A company would take the information that could be useful to an AI, and convert it into a vector database that takes unstructured information and organizes it so similar topics are grouped together. That way, when a prompt is sent to the LLM, it can include all the relevant context.

It’s still a good approach for unstructured data for old-fashioned RAG pipelines, but it tends to result in a lot of material, some of which can confuse the LLM or be dated, and excess content means more tokens, which means higher costs. AI agents tend to make a lot of calls to LLMs, so it’s a bad idea to be too wordy. Plus, knowledge graphs allow agents to find the exact information they need, while the semantic layer gives them the knowledge about what to do with that information.

New York Life Group Benefits Solutions uses both vector databases and knowledge graphs. The knowledge graph it uses is built on top of the LangGraph AI agent framework from LangChain.

“The knowledge graphs work for multi-agent orchestration and the vector database for gen AI RAG applications,” says Matt Marze, the company’s CIO.

The knowledge graphs begin with the basic business information, data, signals, and external data sources, such as information about the broker community. Then the semantic layer includes business understanding, relationships between the data, and common definitions around products and plans, in addition to, he says, the business context of the current situation, history, workflow, and business priorities. “All that drives into insights, predictions, and recommendations, and allows us to coordinate the abilities of the AI agents,” he says.

As agentic AI projects proliferate, the interest in knowledge graphs continues to increase.

“A year and half ago, I was talking about it and people looked at me like I had three heads,” says James Kaplan, distinguished partner at McKinsey & Company. “But in the past year, we’ve seen real uptick for knowledge graphs. Many institutions I know of realize they can use knowledge graphs to support more complicated decision making, and in conjunction with agents, enable more capable agents.”

The flip side

Accuracy and hallucinations are a big problem for AI models in general, but in agentic systems with multiple calls to an LLM, inaccuracies can quickly compound.

“All the models are probabilistic ones,” says Zakir Hussain, partner and EY Americas data and AI leader for industrials and energy. “As soon as you try to use any of those models to answer enterprise-level questions, or questions you want to base your decisions on, they start hallucinating because in many cases they don’t understand or misinterpret the context.”

For business applications in particular, the inaccuracy issue can be a big one, since AI models are trained on generic information. “As soon as it becomes specific to a company, that’s where things start going sideways,” he adds.

According to a paper released at the end of 2025 by researchers at UC Santa Barbara and JP Morgan AI research, knowledge graphs improve accuracy by 26% or more over standard chain-of-thought baselines.

“This whole conversation around ontologies, semantic layers, and knowledge graphs is pretty important right now,” says Hussain.

Every organization is trying to figure out how to leverage AI for growth, efficiency, and productivity, he says. “To be able to unlock these three layers — growth, efficiency, and productivity — you have to codify the context of the company.”

item.title: How BCG turns client innovation into enterprise AI
item.description:
Most CIOs deploy technology created by vendors or developed internally for their own organizations. At Boston Consulting Group, CIO Merim Becirovic operates in a different environment. Every day, the firm’s consultants help clients across industries rethink business processes, redesign operating models, and explore new applications of AI. That gives him and his team visibility into a constant stream of experimentation and innovation happening beyond BCG’s walls.

Rather than viewing those ideas as client work alone, Becirovic embraces the concept of customer zero, applying the most promising capabilities within BCG itself. The result is a powerful feedback loop: client engagements generate new ideas, BCG tests and refines them internally, and the lessons learned strengthen future client work.

In this conversation, Becirovic discusses how BCG scales AI through its Genie platform, gives employees the freedom to experiment safely, and turns emerging ideas into the transformation of how work gets done.

What impact is AI having on businesses?

AI brings an upskill of capability and opportunity to do more with technology than ever before. It’s a fundamental reimagining of how tech enables business. For years, we built systems based on the constraints of technology, because we couldn’t get what we wanted out of performance, storage, data, or networks. IT was expensive so we focused on efficiency.

Then we got off the mainframe and into distributed computing, big data centers, virtualization, and the cloud. While AI has existed for years, we finally built the capacity to apply it.

Until now, technology practitioners have done the technical work because it was too costly to get machines to do it. With AI, they can now do the work of machines, meaning you can free humans to do what we’re good at: creative thinking and using AI as a capability to enable that.

How is BCG applying AI to its own operations?

We use the concept of customer zero, and apply the capabilities we imagine for our clients to ourselves. I’m lucky because I have access to consultants around the world who think hard about how to help our clients answer the same questions we’re asking: How do we become an AI-first company? How should we think about deploying agents in our own organization?

Maybe we want to look at contracting differently or use AI to power our engineering teams. That might be something we do for a client, but I want to promote customer zero so we gain that knowledge and apply it to us. This is how we get better using these foundational models.

When work is changing and new technology is available, there are many more iterations of ideas that might be interesting, and they happen a lot faster. Everybody’s been experimenting with custom GPTs and agents, but only as standalone capabilities. As an enterprise leader, I want to take use cases out of project mode and bring them into enterprise scale without creating technical debt.

What’s an example of a scaled AI capability at BCG?

BCG Genie, which won a 2026 CIO 100 Award, is the platform we use to take AI ideas out of project mode and run them across the enterprise. It gives us one secure place to build, govern, and scale agents and other AI tools, using what we developed for clients through BCG X, the part of BCG that delivers technology and data capabilities.

Today, everything we do to support BCG, from HR to tech support, runs through Genie, with more than 100 use cases. Key to Genie is Spark Lab. You have a spark? Here’s a lab. If you’re a consultant who wants to test whether something’s a good idea, you put it in a sandbox, connect it to additional information in the business, and start to get insights. Then you think about how to roll an idea out to the whole company if it’s really good. Spark Lab provides a self-service idea generation and scaling opportunity for everyone.

Some CIOs will fear people trying technologies that aren’t part of their tech stack. But Spark Lab users don’t use new technologies. They’re consuming patterns from the platform, and we apply security and data controls as the idea scales. We don’t refactor up to our standards later; the standards are there from the start.

What do CIOs need to get right to make AI pay off?

Technically, you need a solid and well running standing in the cloud. But on the people side, it’s giving people agency to use the tools, not just give access to them. We’ve solved so many of the hard problems of technology, our new job is to change the way work is done.

My peers know we’re change leaders now, not just technology leaders. Our vantage point across the business lets us connect the dots and drive transformation.

In a real transformation, 30% is the models and the technology, and 70% is people and processes. Most organizations stop at the 30%. The question is how the 30% affects the 70%, and how you transform and invest in that 70%. That’s how you get compounded benefits.

What’s the difference between alignment and agreement?

You can get alignment, but do you have agreement? We can all align on being AI-first, but agreement means we’ll build these platforms, use these capabilities, transform these workflows, and change the way we work. Without agreement, you get a lot of false starts. It’s a subtle difference, but with AI, it matters more because the work itself is changing. We have to agree on how we take advantage of these capabilities.

What’s your advice for emerging CIOs?

Be hyper curious. Play with all the technology and look at different ways you can bring it together to solve business problems. Even with AI, enterprise technology is hard. It won’t magically connect everything, so understand the trade-offs and complications. We all still need to do the brilliant basics of running an enterprise that serves many different types of work.

The more experience you can get around how technology is delivered, used, reimagined, and applied, and how we evolved to AI, the better set up you’ll be as a next-gen leader, because this stuff is moving so fast.

And remember the 70%. Many companies have paid a lot for half-completed transformations. The technology mostly worked, but something happened in the adoption cycle. Technology will become easier and cheaper to consume. We can make mistakes faster and more cheaply, and refactor code and capabilities. But changing how people work is still an evolving capability, and we must keep investing in it.

item.title: Why IT leaders who hit every target still get passed over for promotion
item.description:
A VP of engineering I coach received a performance review last year full of positive feedback. She met her targets, her manager had nothing but good things to say about her delivery, and the one piece of critical feedback she received was so vague she felt she couldn’t act on it. She was also passed over for the CTO role she’d been working toward. She told me she’d been the obvious choice, and she couldn’t understand why the decision went the other way. Her review said she was doing great work, so she didn’t know what else to do.

I’ve coached more than 1,000 technology professionals one-on-one, and a growing share of my practice is working with CIOs, CTOs and VPs of product and engineering. The pattern she described comes up often with the leaders I support. The leader performs, and the review confirms the results, yet the promotion goes to someone else. The review covers the job they have. The promotion decision is about a job they don’t have yet.

CIO.com has covered why VPs and IT directors with strong delivery records keep missing the CIO chair. In my coaching practice, the problem starts earlier. It shows up the first time an IT leader with a great review gets passed over for promotion and can’t get a straight answer about why.

Let’s explore why strong reviews and promotions measure different things, and what I assign leaders who get passed over, drawing on real examples from my own coaching practice and IT leaders in the industry.

The review and the promotion measure different things

When this client asked her boss why she wasn’t the obvious choice, she got a list of reasons. She agreed with some and disagreed with others. The feedback she didn’t agree with was the same vague feedback she’d received in her review, and nothing on the list told her what to do differently.

I hear some version of this from IT leaders at every level. The review rewards what they delivered over the last cycle, but the promotion decision asks whether the people above them can already picture this person one level up. This disconnect frustrates the leaders I coach, yet it’s how promotions get decided at most companies, large and small.

Ranjith Raghunath, CEO of CX Data Labs and a former leader at Amazon, GSK and Samsung Electronics America, described one of the hardest conversations he had during his time at GSK, when he decided not to promote his IT services coordinator to head of IT. The coordinator was excellent at running the support team, resolving tickets, training employees and handling the thousands of small tasks that keep laptops and software platforms working. The coordinator wanted an executive role. Raghunath told me he couldn’t replace that skill set or the rapport the coordinator had with his team, so the company hired externally for a higher-level, systemic thinker, who worked out well.

The coordinator was doing his current job well. The head of IT job needed different skills, and nothing in his day-to-day work showed he had them. Raghunath also told me his own mistake was failing to communicate clearly with the candidate, who felt let down and believed he was a perfect fit for the role, even though he wasn’t.

A 2026 Enhancv survey of 500 US managers found that 62% credited performance and results as the biggest factor in reaching leadership, and only 6% named education, yet 65% called their degree and credentials essential or very important in getting their current role. Volen Vulkov, Enhancv’s co-founder, told me that when strong people get passed over, they usually do more of what got them noticed in the first place. “More hours, more projects, another certificate. Our data says that’s rarely what’s missing. Almost nobody credited their credentials for their promotion,” he said. “The people deciding are asking a different question: is this person already making the calls the next role needs? So, look at the decisions your manager makes that you don’t. Then ask to take a few of them on.”

Vulkov’s advice matches what I see with my clients. The IT leaders who get promoted tend to be the ones who are already doing pieces of the next job before anyone hands it to them. The leaders who get passed over tend to be doing their current job extremely well and waiting for someone to notice.

Your work can’t speak for itself

My client, the VP of engineering, was convinced she had done enough to earn the promotion to CTO. I pushed back. The executive who hired her and championed her for years had left the company, and her new boss had far less history with her. He saw her as a strong VP, not as a C-suite leader, and that view, not her results, decided the promotion. In a promotion conversation, perception is reality.

A colleague then transferred onto her team from another part of the company and admitted they didn’t know what the team really did. Another executive at the company, they said, seemed to do everything. She disagreed, and she was right to. Her team owned the platform the rest of the company was built upon, while the other team shipped features dependent on her work. The point I made to her afterward was that this person now reported to her and still couldn’t describe the team’s work. If someone on her own team couldn’t, the executives deciding on promotions definitely couldn’t either.

Many of the IT leaders I coach started in roles where the code spoke for itself. The feature shipped or it didn’t. Senior roles don’t work that way. The people making promotion decisions see a fraction of the work, and they fill in the rest from what they hear about it.

What I assigned instead of more hours

When a client is passed over for a promotion, their instinct is often to deliver more, but Vulkov’s data says productivity is rarely what’s missing, and my coaching experience agrees.

With this client, I assigned two pieces of homework.

The first was a mini 360-degree review. She asked her boss and a few peers how well she was bringing them along and how they perceived her team. Their answers gave her more to work with than her formal performance review had. She learned that people couldn’t always follow how she reached her conclusions, so from the outside, her decisions looked like skipped steps.

The second was an internal PR campaign. I asked her to treat the executives around her as her most important stakeholders. In practice, that meant sharing more updates on what her team was building and why, giving more positive feedback to the people around her, hosting internal engineering sessions on where the platform was headed, presenting her team’s work at an all-hands meeting, and saying yes to external speaking engagements alongside other industry leaders so people inside the company saw her name attached to the function.

I assign some version of this homework to most clients who get passed over. The questions in the mini 360 change with the situation, and so do the moves in the PR campaign. The goal doesn’t change. The client stops producing more and starts making the work they’ve already done visible to the people who make decisions.

My client is still at the company and still on the path to the CTO role. She no longer assumes her review will make the case for her, so she makes it herself.

If you’ve just received a strong review and watched the promotion you wanted go to someone else, the review wasn’t wrong. It measured the job you have. Ask the people who decide promotions what they’d need to see from you in the next role, then start doing some of that work now. Tell the people around you what your team does and why it matters, because they’re filling in that story with or without you. The promotion rarely goes to the leader who did the most work. It goes to the one the decision makers can already picture in the job.

item.title: AWS PrivateLink Tunnel Endpoints Open a Whole CIDR Range to Another Account
item.description:
AWS has detailed tunnel endpoints, a PrivateLink endpoint type that gives a consumer VPC access to an entire network segment in another account rather than one resource at a time, over an overlapping address space and with consumer-initiated connections only. The consumer must wrap traffic in GENEVE; only TCP and DNS pass, and access logs cannot attribute traffic to a workload behind the endpoint.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Your agentic AI results can’t be checked. Here’s how to fix that
item.description:
Read 50 published accounts of agentic AI in production and a pattern emerges fast. Escalations down. Handling times down. Conversion up. Onboarding compressed from weeks to days.

Now read them looking for how those numbers were produced, and the field thins out. The window is rarely stated, the denominator almost never and concurrent initiatives that could have produced the same movement go unnamed. You get a number and an implied causal claim, with nothing a skeptic could object to.

This usually isn’t dishonesty. Nobody has told practitioners what a defensible result looks like, so careful and careless accounts read identically.

The cost lands on CIOs. If you’re weighing a major agentic investment, you can’t tell a result achieved at peak trading volume from one achieved in a quiet quarter with the window picked afterward. Both show up as a percentage.

I recently completed an 18-month deployment of 25 production agents across a large travel and cruise group. I’ve written about the strategy and the domain-tuned small models behind it, but not how far its numbers can be trusted. Here is the standard I now hold them to, and the operational failure that undermines every metric if you miss it.

Five ways deployments corrupt their own measurement

  1. The denominator moves. An agent reduces escalations. So does a quiet quarter. A rate without its volume is a way of declining to say which happened.
  2. The window is chosen after the fact. A steadily improving agent always has some recent window in which it looks better than any earlier one, and research on analytical flexibility shows how easily that produces apparently strong findings from nothing. The tell: when one account reports three outcomes over three different periods, the periods were fitted to the outcomes.
  3. The baseline contains slack. Automate a manual process and you usually clear its backlog at the same time, so the comparison measures a faster process and a one-off vanished queue at once.
  4. The change is never alone. Organizations willing to deploy autonomous agents are usually already in motion: a platform rebuild, a repricing, a reorganization. Year-over-year comparison controls for seasonality, and for none of that.
  5. The definition is proprietary. A “Tier 1 escalation” in your own platform means whatever your queue classification says, and isn’t comparable with a competitor’s figure, though both appear as percentages.

CLEAR: Five tests for a reportable result

The NIST AI Risk Management Framework and ISO/IEC 42001 tell you to measure, not what a reportable number looks like. CLEAR sits beneath them and needs only ordinary operational records and one discipline: decide before you know the result.

  1. C: Concurrent changes registered. What else changed in the same window, and could it independently produce the result?
  2. L: Locked window. Was the period fixed before the result was known, and does it include your hardest trading conditions?
  3. E: Evidentiary custody. Which system produced the count, who defines the category and who reviewed the figure?
  4. A: Attributable baseline. How much of the gain came from re-engineering the process, and how much from clearing accumulated slack?
  5. R: Reference volume. Did the underlying volume hold steady, and is that stated?

Four tests ask for disclosure, which is cheap. The locked window asks for pre-commitment, which is costly because it forecloses discovering later that a different period tells a better story. In my experience, it does most of the work.

Medicine and ML research already have reporting standards such as CONSORT-AI and REFORMS; agentic deployments don’t. CLEAR isn’t a validity standard, though: a result that passes all five is still a single-organization observation. It gives you an account a skeptic can attack.

Naren Gangavarapu

Applying it to my own results

We used three outcomes internally to justify further investment. Two came out weaker under CLEAR.

Tier 1 support escalations fell 34%

This largely survives. The six-month window was fixed to include peak season, contact volume was flat year over year and counts came from the system of record, reviewed by finance rather than the agent team. With volume flat, falling demand can’t explain the drop. What doesn’t survive: Tier 1 is our own classification, so the absolute figure can’t be compared across organizations.

Operator onboarding fell from 23 days to 3

The baseline isn’t attributable. The 23 days included time in a standing backlog, and part of the gain came from clearing that queue, not shortening the process. It shows a process re-engineered and a queue eliminated, not a like-for-like comparison.

Booking conversion rose 24%

The weakest of the three. A marketplace rebuild and opt-in dynamic pricing ran in the same window as the AI-native search capability credited with most of the uplift. Reported without that caveat, it would be the most impressive number here and the least informative.

Two of three carrying material qualifications is probably typical. A result that survives disclosure of its weaknesses is worth more than one never tested.

The failure that makes everything else moot

CLEAR assumes the operational record is complete. In agentic systems, one gap quietly breaks that assumption.

The most important control in our deployment cost nothing to build. Any line-of-business manager, from the wholesale desk to the cruise operations floor, could stop an agent within ninety seconds. No ticket, no approval. If the manager was wrong, we restarted the agent and discussed it at the next recalibration session. Being wrong cost an hour of throughput; being slow could cost a customer.

A manager using that control is the system working as designed. The failure is the override that isn’t logged. The record that would have shown a tolerance band was miscalibrated never exists, and the agent’s statistics are computed over a population from which a conscientious human has removed the hard cases.

Every downstream metric improves. Escalation rates fall because escalations were intercepted first. Confidence scores look strong because low-confidence decisions were pulled out by hand. Exception reports look clean. The organization believes its agents perform better than they do, and its results become unfalsifiable, because the basis was corrupted before anyone thought to write it down.

This echoes Lisanne Bainbridge’s 1983 “ironies of automation”: the human handles what the designer couldn’t automate, with no way to feed that judgment back into the design. No care at write-up time recovers a record that was never captured. Measurement in agentic systems is a daily operating discipline, not a reporting exercise.

Six practices that keep the record intact

We treated agents as high-volume junior team members: fast, tireless and capable of significant harm if poorly supervised. You wouldn’t put a new hire on the floor without onboarding and an escalation path, and agents are no different. Every manager with agents adopted six habits:

  1. A five-minute morning review of overnight agent activity, treated as a floor walk.
  2. A weekly scorecard written for operations, not technologists: completion, escalation rate, decision confidence.
  3. An exception-first culture that asks what the agent flagged as uncertain, not only what it did.
  4. Explicit human-agent teaming norms: when a human overrides, when they defer and how it’s logged.
  5. Scenario playbooks for the ten likeliest failure modes, owned by operations.
  6. A monthly recalibration session reviewing tolerance limits against incident data.

The fourth carries the most weight and gets the least attention. The sixth is how the organization learns, by asking what fired that shouldn’t have and what didn’t fire that should have. Both are answerable only if the override record is complete.

One design decision supports all six: we allocated autonomy by reversibility, not risk appetite. Non-technologists can classify reversibility at design time, and it maps straight to a control: the less reversible the action, the earlier a human must stand in the loop. Of our 25 agents, seven could act without confirmation. Thirteen either required it or were barred from autonomous external communication.

Where this won’t work

If you ship agent changes weekly, there’s no stable intervention to lock a window around; report rolling comparisons and say so. If the agent does work nobody did before, name the tests that don’t apply instead of quietly dropping them. Disclosure has commercial cost: we withheld volumes but disclosed the comparison basis. And disciplined reporters will look weaker than those who aren’t, a coordination problem no one practitioner can solve.

What to do on Monday

Check whether human overrides of agent decisions are logged. Inspect the log; don’t just ask whether one exists. If overrides aren’t captured, no performance figure you hold about your agents means what it appears to.

Then, before the next reporting cycle, lock your measurement window and write it down: the period, the denominator and everything else changing in the same interval. That costs nothing in advance and is impossible afterward. Then ask of every result: what would make a reader disbelieve this, and have I said so?

The organizations that scale agentic AI won’t have the best models; capability is converging and procurable. The operational habits around it aren’t, and they took us eighteen months to build. The technology was the easy part. The measurement was the work.

item.title: After Black October, OffSec Turns PHPH2Shell and Other New Vulnerabilities Into Hands-On Labs
item.description:
OffSec built 14 labs on real CVEs in two weeks. Its Level 20 offer takes $550 off Learn One for learners ready to train against threats like these.

OffSec, the world’s leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe. The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw at the center of the month’s disclosure wave.

Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models. Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure. CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers. CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits. An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it.

“AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers,” said Alex “Sickness” Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. “Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week. An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself.”

OffSec’s new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include:

  • Offensive Labs built on recent CVEs in Kestra, Hermes WebUI, WordPress 7.0.2, the Algernon web server and a chained Vite and Uptime Kuma exposure.
  • Defensive Labs where learners secure vulnerable versions of Spring, Kestra and Next.js.
  • Incident Investigations modeled on real attack types. These include ransomware that began with a help desk call, an email compromise that rerouted a client payment, a breached SSL VPN appliance and an intrusion at a hydroelectric plant.
  • AI Targets such as an AI-driven tool marketplace with an automated reviewer and agent.

OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm.

“These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more,” said CEO Wang. “You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it. When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It’s no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Level 20: Same Game, New Level

OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20, a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027. Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer. Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents.

  • 365 days of course and lab access
